doc: Texts of data.json that followed the Coral Finder 2022 book too closely, reworded in the app's own words (tools/apply_book_rewrite.py). 'old' is a hash of the old wording, 'old5' the hashes of its 5-word runs (tests/booktext.test.js): no book text is kept here.

rewrites.new: Branches studded with lumps of skeleton (verrucae) that make them look knobbly.
Short, stocky branches; their tips are blunt, sometimes a little flattened, as though pinched.
Slender branches that barely narrow towards the tip and end round or club-shaped.
Next to Montipora, its corallites are a little bigger and sharper in outline.
Each corallite is a tube with tall, thin walls and a plain outside: no costae, no decoration.
Its tube-shaped corallites bristle with septa that stick out like blades or spines, an easy giveaway.
The skeleton between corallites is plain and smooth, never ornamented.
Colonies form domes, flat tops or solid masses from stalks that keep forking (phaceloid).
Fine, evenly spaced septo-costae cross each valley square-on, giving a fingerprint look.
Leafy plates with parallel valleys, each crossed square-on by fine, even ribs: a fingerprint look.
All septa the same size, set at even gaps: a zipper pattern.
Tall tentacular lobes stand up from the larger septa, above the disc surface.
Walls can be hard to read: one colony may mix shared and separate walls, with a shadow line between its roundish corallites.
Grows as meandering valleys (flabello-meandroid) or on stalks (phaceloid); each corallite keeps its own wall.
Grows as meandering valleys (flabello-meandroid) or on stalks (phaceloid); each corallite keeps its own wall.
Shape shifts with wave exposure, from columns and branches to ridges and, where roughest, thin crusts.
Shape shifts with wave exposure, from columns and branches to ridges and, where roughest, thin crusts.
Usually a telling cream-brown; the surface is a jumble of small round corallites, 1-2 mm.
Axial corallites, if any, are faint and may come several together; a close relative of Acropora.
Flat fronds that fork, twisted tangles, or plates.
Flat fronds that fork, twisted tangles, or plates.
Corallites on a single face of each frond (unifacial), joined by smooth septo-costae and often leaning towards the edge.
Coral Finder p. 57: in Pavona cactus both faces of a frond carry corallites
A colony resting free on the seabed: fragile, uneven thin sheets or domes reaching 70 cm.
A colony resting free on the seabed: fragile, uneven thin sheets or domes reaching 70 cm.
Corallites hard to make out; septal teeth tall; septo-costae often cross at right angles.
The skeleton is light and brittle and often lies in heaps of stacked broken pieces.
A colony lying loose, round, oval or uneven, up to 40 cm; the skeleton is heavy with thick walls, its dome high or low.
A colony lying loose, round, oval or uneven, up to 40 cm; the skeleton is heavy with thick walls, its dome high or low.
Blades or thin clubs edged white along the top; each 1 mm corallite sits in a ring of tinier pores.
White or see-through polyps, 8 feathery tentacles; brownish-grey tissue often hides the blue skeleton.
Masses or thick crusts of upright tubes tied together by flat cross-plates; each polyp has 8 feathery tentacles.
The red skeleton is usually covered and shows once the polyps pull back.
Septa trace wavy lines across the surface; septal teeth small.
Coral Finder p. 64: Lobactis looks alike but is oval, its tentacular lobes bigger
Coral Finder p. 46: Echinopora's corallites are denser and more regular
Branching colonies, tight or irregular; 8-15 mm corallites on stalks, sometimes joined in short meanders.
Branching colonies, tight or irregular; 8-15 mm corallites on stalks, sometimes joined in short meanders.
Strong septa and costae show through the tissue; septal teeth small.
Lies loose, 10-30 cm; a fleshy mantle hides its meandering, separate-walled valleys.
Lies loose, 10-30 cm; a fleshy mantle hides its meandering, separate-walled valleys.
Big, thick, lobed teeth show through clear, bubbly tissue; paliform lobes wide.
Colours often stand out; found on walls, the lower slopes and patches between reefs.
A single loose polyp, round or almost, usually 3-8 cm; septal teeth fine.
A single loose polyp, round or almost, usually 3-8 cm; septal teeth fine.
Coral Finder p. 67: easily taken for a young Fungia
Coral Finder p. 67: easily taken for a young Lithophyllon
Platygyra's valleys are smaller and narrower; Pectinia's walls are higher and less tapered.
Round, shallow 3-4 mm corallites; the costae can draw clear patterns; paliform lobes show.
Bigger corallites than Cyphastrea or Astreopora, with none of their beads or spinules.
3-5 mm corallites of uneven shape and size, parted by a groove with small knobs (tubercles).
Wedge septa clearly alternate big and small; mostly pale cream to yellow.
Thin to thick crusts or sub-massive, some with knobs.
Thin to thick crusts or sub-massive, some with knobs.
A Porites look-alike with spines; hides on walls and in shady cave mouths.
From small single polyps or short stalks to flabello-meandroid colonies.
From small single polyps or short stalks to flabello-meandroid colonies.
Walls separate; septal teeth big, blunt and lobed.
Grainy septo-costae make petal-like "flowers"; the surface is dimpled.
Walls faint or missing; septo-costae join the corallites
Septo-costae run on from one corallite to the next
Blue, fire and organ pipe corals, lace corals, spiculites
No symbiotic algae: tube-shaped corallites with tall, thin, plain walls (no costae) on a smooth coenosteum; shaded overhangs.
Corallites without walls, 2-4 mm, set between sharp ridges and joined by smooth septo-costae; fronds often carry them on both faces.
In Pavona cactus both faces of a frond carry corallites; Leptoseris has fewer.
